A2.text:
Grandmother Sona is seventy-four. She was a teacher for forty years. Now she is retired and lives on a small pension. She has white hair and many wrinkles, but she is young at heart.

Last month, Sona joined a dance class at the cultural centre. She goes every Tuesday and Thursday.

Her grandson, Tural, was not happy. “Grandma, please act your age,” he said. “You are over the hill. Dancing is for young people.”

Sona smiled. “Your generation thinks old people should only sit and watch TV,” she said.

Sona has a good friend, Halima. Halima lives in a care home. She has memory loss. Sometimes she forgets the names of her children. Sona visits her every Sunday.

One Sunday, Sona played old music on her phone. Halima stood up. She started to dance! She remembered every step from fifty years ago.

The nurses were very surprised. “Can you come every week and dance with everyone?” they asked.

Now Sona teaches dance at the care home every Sunday. Twenty old people dance with her.

Tural came to watch one day. He saw his grandmother and Halima laughing and dancing. He felt ashamed.

“I'm sorry, Grandma,” he said. “In our family, we must respect elders. And you have a lot of wisdom.”

B1.text:
When Sona retired after forty years of teaching literature in Sumgait, everyone expected her to slow down. She had her pension, her balcony full of geraniums and, at seventy-four, the right to rest. Instead, she signed up for a dance class at the local cultural centre.

Her grandson Tural was horrified when he saw the video she posted. “Grandma, you have to act your age,” he told her. “People will laugh. Let's be honest — you're a bit over the hill for this.”

Sona laughed so hard she had to put her tea down. “Every generation thinks it invented fun,” she said. “I'm old on the outside, my dear. I'm young at heart.”

Every Sunday, Sona visited her oldest friend, Halima, who lived in a care home near the seafront. Halima suffered from memory loss. On bad days, she didn't recognise her own daughter.

One Sunday, hoping to cheer her up, Sona played an old song on her phone — a waltz they used to dance to at student parties fifty years earlier. Halima listened, closed her eyes and slowly stood up. Then, to the astonishment of everyone in the room, she began to dance. Every step was perfect. Her feet remembered what her mind had forgotten.

The nurses gathered at the door. Before Sona left, the manager asked if she would come back and dance with the other residents.

Now, every Sunday afternoon, the care home's dining room becomes a dance floor. Twenty residents move to music from their youth, with Sona leading them in her best shoes.

One Sunday, Tural came along to drive her. He stood at the back and watched his grandmother waltzing with Halima, both of them laughing like girls.

On the way home, he was quiet for a long time. Then he said, “I'm sorry about what I said. I was taught to respect elders, and I forgot. You've got more wisdom than my whole university.”

Sona patted his hand. “Next week,” she said, “you're dancing too.”

B2.text:
When Sona retired after four decades of teaching literature in Sumgait, the general expectation was that she would ease gracefully into stillness — a modest pension, a balcony of geraniums, the well-earned right to do nothing at seventy-four. Instead, within a month, she had enrolled in a ballroom dance class at the cultural centre.

Her grandson Tural, a second-year economics student, discovered this via a video she had posted online and was mortified. “Grandma, with respect, you need to act your age,” he told her. “People will make fun of you. Let's be realistic — you're slightly over the hill for the foxtrot.”

Sona laughed so hard she had to set her tea glass down. “Every generation believes it invented joy,” she replied. “The wrinkles are on the outside, my darling. I'm young at heart.”

Every Sunday, Sona visited her oldest friend, Halima, now living in a care home overlooking the sea. Halima suffered from severe memory loss. On bad days, she looked at her own daughter as if at a polite stranger; on good days, she could recall 1975 in vivid detail while last Tuesday vanished without a trace.

One Sunday, hoping to reach her, Sona played a song on her phone — a waltz they had danced to at student parties half a century earlier. Halima listened with closed eyes, then rose unsteadily from her chair and began, with flawless precision, to dance. Her feet remembered everything her mind had lost.

Nurses gathered silently in the doorway, several wiping their eyes. Before Sona left, the manager asked, almost shyly, whether she might return to dance with the other residents.

Now, every Sunday afternoon, the dining room is transformed into a ballroom. Twenty residents, some in wheelchairs, sway to the music of their youth, led by Sona in her best shoes.

One week Tural reluctantly drove her there and stood at the back of the room, watching his grandmother waltz with Halima, the two of them giggling like schoolgirls.

He said nothing for most of the journey home. Finally, staring at the road, he murmured, “I owe you an apology. I was brought up to respect elders, and somehow I forgot. You have more wisdom than my entire faculty.”

Sona patted his hand. “Apology accepted,” she said. “Next Sunday, you're wearing your good shoes.”
